title: Service Stress Profiles and Dimensioned Error-Budget Playbook
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview

This playbook defines a compact, operationally actionable framework for pairing service-specific stress profiles with a multi-dimensional (dimensioned) error-budget model. The goal is to give SRE, oncall, and platform teams clear, deterministic actions at well-defined error-budget and capacity signal thresholds so we can: preserve customer-facing SLAs, avoid expensive over-provisioning, and make graceful, predictable tradeoffs during stress events.

Key objectives
- Provide a taxonomy of Service Stress Profiles (SSP) to categorize services by their dominant operational modes.
- Define Dimensioned Error Budgets (DEB) — separate budget accounting for latency, availability, and correctness/quality — and prescribe remediation actions per dimension.
- Tie DEB thresholds to capacity policies, autoscale behavior, and SLO-aware mitigations.
- Offer runbooks (preventative and reactive) and sample alert/telemetry rules to minimize ambiguity during incidents.

Scope
- Applies to all production-facing Redwood services that host or orchestrate model inference and control-plane operations (hosted API, Dedicated routing, Private control plane).
- Not intended for low-risk internal tooling unless explicitly onboarded.

Definitions
- SLI (Service Level Indicator): a measurable signal (e.g., p99 latency for generation requests, 5xx rate for control-plane writes).
- SLO (Service Level Objective): target on an SLI with a time window (e.g., 99% requests < 250ms over 30d).
- Dimensioned Error Budget (DEB): error budget tracked independently across dimensions: latency, availability, and correctness. Each dimension has its own budget consumption and remediation ladder.
- Service Stress Profile (SSP): a named class describing operational behavior and primary failure modes for a service (see taxonomy below).

Service Stress Profile taxonomy
1) Interactive low-latency ("LL-Interactive")
   - Examples: chat generation, text-completion API for synchronous UX.
   - Primary SLI: p95/p99 tail latency (server processing time), warm-cache hit ratio.
   - Typical capacity signals: inference GPU saturation % (kernel_util), queue depth, KV cache hit ratio.

2) High-throughput streaming ("HT-Stream")
   - Examples: bulk embedding streams, long token streams for transcription.
   - Primary SLI: sustained throughput, per-token cost, stable tail latency under continuous load.
   - Capacity signals: memory pressure for KV caches, I/O throughput (NVMe), batching efficiency.

3) Background batch / offline ("Batch-Async")
   - Examples: nightly indexing, offline evals, model conversion jobs.
   - Primary SLI: job completion rate, job success ratio, median job runtime.
   - Capacity signals: queued jobs, backoff retries, preemptible GPU eviction rates.

4) Control plane / provisioning ("Control-Plane")
   - Examples: model rollout API, billing, quota management.
   - Primary SLI: write availability (5m), leader election latency, consistent state propagation.
   - Capacity signals: DB replica lag, write throughput saturation, request queueing.

Dimensioned Error Budget model
- Each SLO is expressed as: SLO{name, SLI, window, target}. For every SLO we track a percentage of budget consumed per window.
- DEB maintains a separate budget for: latency, availability, correctness/quality. A single incident may consume one or more budgets.

Example: "LL-Interactive" service SLOs (30d window)
- Availability SLO: success_rate >= 99.95% (errors exclude client input validation).
- Latency SLO: p99 latency < 350ms for model-generation endpoints.
- Correctness SLO: prompt-template-regression tests pass >= 98% on sampled golden prompts.

Budget calculation (simple)
- For Availability budget: budget_remaining = (target_success_rate - observed_failure_rate) / (1 - observed_failure_rate). We normalize to percent remaining.
- For Latency budget: compute fraction of requests that violated latency threshold over the window; budget_remaining = 1 - violation_fraction.
- For Correctness budget: use regression test failure fraction on sampled checks.

Dimensioned threshold ladder and actions
- Green (>= 70% budget remaining) — normal ops. No special actions.
- Yellow (40%–69% remaining) — advisory. Notify product oncall + run targeted mitigations (see runbook).
- Orange (10%–39% remaining) — elevated. Pause non-essential background jobs, enable aggressive autoscale, reduce tenant burst allowances, start capacity hedging.
- Red (<10% remaining) — emergency. Initiate SLO-preserving mode (fall back to smaller models, hard-rate-limit lower-priority tiers, divert traffic to healthy regions or Dedicated pools).

Table: example DEB thresholds and primary action (plain-text table)
| dimension | green | yellow | orange | red | primary action |
| Availability | >=70% | 40–69% | 10–39% | <10% | reroute/activate-fallbacks |
| Latency | >=70% | 40–69% | 10–39% | <10% | dynamic-batching/trim-seq-length |
| Correctness | >=70% | 40–69% | 10–39% | <10% | rollback-model/disable-regression-affected-flows |

Operational runbooks
A. Preventative (daily/weekly checks)
1. Daily quick health (oncall morning check, 5–10 minutes):
   - Verify p99 latency and availability for top-3 customer routes.
   - Confirm autoscale headroom: average node GPU_util < 60% and queue depth < 30% for LL-Interactive services.
   - Run a short golden-prompt regression for correctness dimension (10 random prompts).
   - Commands: 
     - curl -s "https://<service>/healthz" | jq .status
     - redwoodctl capacity list --service <svc> --format=table
2. Weekly capacity sanity: run a capacity-simulation against the canary pool (see "Capacity planning" section).

B. Reactive (error budget consumption triggers)
Trigger: any dimension crosses into Orange or Red.
Orange steps (10–39% remaining):
1. Page oncall (primary SRE) and product oncall; include DEB context and the top affected tenants.
2. Throttle or pause background jobs: kubectl -n infra scale job/<batch-job-name> --replicas=0 or disable via job scheduler.
3. Increase autoscale aggressiveness: redwoodctl autoscale set --service <svc> --policy aggressive --min-instances <n> --max-instances <m>.
4. Temporarily reduce per-tenant burst allowance: update rate-limit-policy via admin console or API.
5. If latency dimension, enable per-request KV-cache idiomatic warm path: set header X-Cache-Warm: true for canary.
6. Record mitigation steps in the incident ticket and monitor DEB for 30m after changes.

Red steps (<10% remaining):
1. Execute graceful degradation policy for the SSP class: for LL-Interactive prefer model-fallback -> routing to Dedicated pools -> rate-limits; for HT-Stream prefer batching optimizations and non-blocking accept-queues.
2. If fallback to smaller model: perform canary routing (10% traffic) to canary model; if metrics look stable after 15m, promote.
3. Activate cross-region reroute: update traffic-routing policy to route X% of traffic to region with spare capacity.
4. For correctness regressions, perform immediate model rollback and disable the offending model tag across deployments.
5. Mobilize incident bridge and follow Incident Review Standards.

Escalation matrix and ownership
- Primary SRE owner: listed in service manifest (manifest.owner). If not found contact "platform-sre@redwood.com".
- Product oncall: product-team-of-service (also in manifest).
- Tier-2 engineering: runtime and inference team for model/kernel issues; storage team for KV/NS issues.

Capacity planning and simulation cadence
- Capacity simulations frequency: monthly for each SSP; weekly for LL-Interactive during high-growth periods.
- Simulation inputs: 95/99 percentile request volume growth, sequence length distribution shifts, tenant concentration scenarios.
- Surge hedges: pre-allocated buffer expressed in GPU-minutes: default 20% for LL-Interactive, 10% for HT-Stream. These are allocated by redwoodctl capacity earmark --service <svc> --minutes <n>.

Table: capacity tags and hedging policy
| SSP | suggested buffer | autoscale policy | earmark label |
| LL-Interactive | 20% | latency-first (fast scale-up) | hedge-ll-interactive |
| HT-Stream | 10% | throughput-first (gradual) | hedge-ht-stream |
| Batch-Async | 0–5% | batch-windowed | hedge-batch |
| Control-Plane | 15% | availability-first | hedge-controlplane |

Alerting and telemetry examples
- Minimal telemetry needed per service: p50/p95/p99 latency, success_rate (2xx/5xx split), queue_depth, gpu_util, cache_hit_ratio, regression_test_failure_rate.
- Example Prometheus-style alert (pseudo-YAML):
  - alert: HighP99LatencyLLInteractive
    expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)) > 0.35
    for: 5m
    labels: {severity: page, team: platform-sre}
    annotations: {summary: "p99 latency > 350ms for LL-Interactive"}

- DEB dashboard slices: current budget by dimension, 30d burn rate, top contributing tenants, recent mitigation actions.

Runbook templates (incident ticket seed)
- Title: [DEB][<dimension>][<svc>] <short description>
- Priority: P1/P2 per DEB color
- Fields to populate: observed_metric, window, budget_remaining, top_5_tenants_by_impact, mitigation_steps_taken, time_of_first_action, rollback_actions.

Integration with post-incident reviews
- For any Orange/Red event that required mitigations, follow Incident Review Standards: collect SLI timeseries 24h before and after, capture deployment timeline, config changes, capacity allocation events, and DEB consumption graphs.
- Include a remediation story and capacity follow-up owner with ETA.

Appendix A — sample SLO snippets (copyable text)
- Availability SLO (30d): success_rate >= 99.95%
- Latency SLO (30d): p99(request_duration_seconds) < 0.350
- Correctness SLO (30d): regression_pass_rate >= 98% on golden prompt set sampled daily

Appendix B — sample mitigation CLI snippets
- Pause batch jobs: kubectl -n jobs scale job/batch-indexer --replicas=0
- Earmark capacity: redwoodctl capacity earmark --service inference-ll --minutes 1200 --label hedge-ll-interactive
- Toggle autoscale policy: redwoodctl autoscale set --service inference-ll --policy latency-first --cooldown 60s

Appendix C — capacity simulation checklist
1. Define scenario (growth %, seq-length change, top-tenant spike).
2. Replay representative traces for 30m sustained window.
3. Measure p99, queue depth, GPU kernel_util, KV hit ratios.
4. Validate DEB post-simulation and adjust earmarks.

Related documentation
- Service posture and capacity playbook (see related_pages).
- SLO rollout and canary gating standards.
- Incident review evidence collection guidance.

Ownership and maintenance
- Owner: Platform SRE (oncall rotation).
- Review cadence: bi-annual review aligned to product roadmap updates or after any Red DEB event.
- How to request onboarding: open a request labeled "onboard-deb" in the platform-sre project board and include the service manifest and expected traffic profile.

Notes and rationale
- We use separate budgets to avoid masking correctness regressions with good availability (and vice versa). This reduces high-cost rollbacks that have low customer-impact tradeoffs.
- The SSP taxonomy intentionally focuses on dominant operational levers so mitigation playbooks can be succinct and consistent across teams.
